## Search method v007

Define X and Y exactly, including entity unit, exclusions, effective dates, eligible subtypes and group-membership rules. Start sequentially with one X-only search, one Y-only search and one conjunction search, using the user's broad predicate wording rather than a familiar subtype. Maintain deduplicated X/Y frontiers and an identity/evidence ledger. Also maintain a compact scope ledger: for each discovery query record added restrictions not required by the hunt (subtype, occupation, geography, era, source or familiar-name terms). A successful restricted query does not establish coverage of its parent category. Derive a few meaningful sibling partitions from source taxonomies or the eligibility definition; do not invent an exhaustive cross-product or enumerate a whole census by default. Run short discovery/check rounds, prioritizing expected verified additions per total resolution cost. Each round's neglected-subtype or reverse-frontier probe must address a specific untested scope-ledger cell or remove a recorded accidental restriction; merely paraphrasing a prior conjunction does not qualify. Check source-backed candidates on Parallel for only unresolved predicates, supplying identity and existing evidence. Use small affordable batches, price every candidate, and do not recheck established facts. No result means unresolved, not false; reject only on contradiction or an exhaustive applicable source. Escalate promising ambiguous or conflicting cases individually to Exa. After two discovery searches add no plausible identities, prohibit synonymous conjunction searches and perform a residual-scope pass: identify the most consequential restriction accumulated so far, try a sibling subtype or unrestricted parent on the opposite frontier, then resolve resulting candidates before further discovery. Reserve at least 35% of initial funds for evidence and stop discovery whenever pending checks require the remaining funds. Before submitting with spare funds, perform up to three affordable residual probes covering distinct untested restrictions or source partitions, retaining enough funds to verify their likely candidates. Stop this pass after two probes add neither candidates nor useful evidence; do not spend merely to exhaust the budget. Finish with identity, predicate, subtype and effective-date audits; submit supported intersections only and never infer completeness from saturation.

### Routing policy
Default route: providers ['parallel'], tier default, 8 results per provider.
check_candidates route: ['parallel'].
Parallel alone, default tier, 8 results for baseline and residual discovery, 4 for exact missing-fact checks. No routine also variants or broad auto-routing. Price candidate batches as the sum of queries and provider charges; fewer results are not presumed cheaper. Exa alone with 4 results for selected unresolved identities where ambiguity, conflicting evidence or inaccessibility warrants the higher cost. At most one initial Exa discovery probe after Parallel stagnation, continued only if it contributes useful new identities or evidence. Try a genuinely different scope partition on Parallel before buying provider diversity for a repetitive query. Authoritative-domain filters are for targeted evidence, not general frontier coverage; relax failed filters. Use publication-date filters only when publication date itself determines eligibility, and verify effective dates in content.

### Fetch policy
Reuse cached source facts. Fetch authoritative pages that can settle missing identity or predicates, and useful multi-candidate lists, rather than every result. When a list is used for scope coverage, inspect its stated subtype, date range and pagination/section links; an excerpt or one section is not an exhausted category. Follow only sections tied to a promising uncovered partition, without committing to bulk census extraction. After a blocked or uninformative page, make one targeted alternate-source attempt rather than a fetch chain.

## SiftText

SiftText is persistent memory across chats.

Entry: /Users/jack/sifttext/nodes/5e565245-14fe-406c-977c-cf94a9be246b/node.md
Retrieval guide: /Users/jack/sifttext/nodes/526ed0f5-4e5d-42b3-9e3f-b7ad429f2df8/node.md

At the start of every new chat, unless I say not to use SiftText, before any other tool call:
1. Run `sifttext instructions`.
2. Read the Entry above and follow it, plus any `agent-instructions` the command returns.
3. Before retrieving knowledge, read the Retrieval guide above, do not search first.

## Tooling policy

- Never directly invoke `python`, `python3`, `pip`, or `pip3` unless explicitly instructed by the human.
- Use `uv` for all agent-initiated Python work:
  - Python execution: `uv run python ...`
  - Scripts and tests: `uv run ...`
  - Throwaway dependencies: `uv run --with <package> ...`
  - Python CLI tools: `uvx <tool>`
  - Durable project dependencies: use the project's appropriate `uv` command and preserve its lockfile.
- For non-Python probing or testing with unavailable tools:
  - One executable: `nix run nixpkgs#<package> -- <args>`
  - Temporary environment: `nix shell nixpkgs#<package> ... --command <command>`
- Nix environments are temporary, but downloaded store paths may remain cached until garbage collection.
- If a Nix dependency becomes useful for recurring or future work, tell the human and suggest adding it to the appropriate durable Nix configuration (such as a project flake/dev shell, Home Manager, or nix-darwin configuration). Do not make that durable change unless asked.

</addendum>

Appearance

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

* Lunar: 1,624 craters (31.2%)
* Martian: 1,092 craters (21.0%)
* Venusian: 900 craters (17.3%)
* Mercurian: 397 craters (7.6%)
* Others: 1,198 craters (23.0%)

Distribution of named [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") in the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") as of 2017.

This is a **list of craters on Mars**. [Impact craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars "Mars") larger than 1 km (0.62 mi) exist by the hundreds of thousands, but only about one thousand of them have names.[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-1) Names are assigned by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") after petitioning by relevant scientists, and in general, only craters that have a significant research interest are given names. Martian craters are named after famous scientists and [science fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_fiction "Science fiction") authors, or if less than 60 km (37 mi) in diameter, after towns on [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth"). Craters cannot be named for living people, and names for small craters are rarely intended to commemorate a specific town.[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Categories-2) Latitude and longitude are given as planetographic coordinates with west longitude.

## Statistics

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=List_of_craters_on_Mars&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Statistics")]

As of 2017, Martian craters account for 21% of all 5,211 named craters in the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System"). Apart from the [Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moon "Moon"), no other body has as many named craters as Mars. Other, non-planetary bodies with numerous named craters include [Callisto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Callisto_(moon) "Callisto (moon)") ([141](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Callisto "List of craters on Callisto")), [Ganymede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ganymede_(moon) "Ganymede (moon)") ([131](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Ganymede "List of craters on Ganymede")), [Rhea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhea_(moon) "Rhea (moon)") (128), [Vesta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4_Vesta "4 Vesta") (90), [Ceres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceres_(dwarf_planet) "Ceres (dwarf planet)") (90), [Dione](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dione_(moon) "Dione (moon)") (73), [Iapetus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iapetus_(moon) "Iapetus (moon)") (58), [Enceladus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enceladus_(moon) "Enceladus (moon)") (53), [Tethys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tethys_(moon) "Tethys (moon)") (50) and [Europa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa_(moon) "Europa (moon)") ([41](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Europa "List of craters on Europa")). For a full list, *see [List of craters in the Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_in_the_Solar_System "List of craters in the Solar System")*. The total number of craters on Mars greater than 1 kilometre in diameter is approximately 385,000, with 21% of those (~85,000) being over 3 kilometers in diameter.[[3]](#cite_note-3) The number of craters on Mars over 25 metres in diameter is suggested to be approximately 90 million.[[4]](#cite_note-4)

### Largest craters

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=List_of_craters_on_Mars&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Largest craters")]

Some of the largest craters on Mars remain unnamed. Diameters differ depending on source data. The largest confirmed impact basins on Mars are [Utopia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utopia_Planitia "Utopia Planitia") (buried, estimated diameter 3,300 km) [Hellas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hellas_Planitia "Hellas Planitia") (2,300 km), [Argyre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argyre_Planitia "Argyre Planitia") ( 1,800 km) and [Isidis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isidis_Planitia "Isidis Planitia") (1,500 km).

Appearance

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

* Lunar: 1,624 craters (31.2%)
* Martian: 1,092 craters (21.0%)
* Venusian: 900 craters (17.3%)
* Mercurian: 397 craters (7.6%)
* Others: 1,198 craters (23.0%)

Distribution of named [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") in the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") as of 2017.

This is a **list of craters on Mars**. [Impact craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars "Mars") larger than 1 km (0.62 mi) exist by the hundreds of thousands, but only about one thousand of them have names.[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-1) Names are assigned by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") after petitioning by relevant scientists, and in general, only craters that have a significant research interest are given names. Martian craters are named after famous scientists and [science fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_fiction "Science fiction") authors, or if less than 60 km (37 mi) in diameter, after towns on [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth"). Craters cannot be named for living people, and names for small craters are rarely intended to commemorate a specific town.[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Categories-2) Latitude and longitude are given as planetographic coordinates with west longitude.

## Statistics

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=List_of_craters_on_Mars&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Statistics")]

As of 2017, Martian craters account for 21% of all 5,211 named craters in the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System"). Apart from the [Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moon "Moon"), no other body has as many named craters as Mars. Other, non-planetary bodies with numerous named craters include [Callisto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Callisto_(moon) "Callisto (moon)") ([141](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Callisto "List of craters on Callisto")), [Ganymede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ganymede_(moon) "Ganymede (moon)") ([131](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Ganymede "List of craters on Ganymede")), [Rhea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhea_(moon) "Rhea (moon)") (128), [Vesta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4_Vesta "4 Vesta") (90), [Ceres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceres_(dwarf_planet) "Ceres (dwarf planet)") (90), [Dione](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dione_(moon) "Dione (moon)") (73), [Iapetus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iapetus_(moon) "Iapetus (moon)") (58), [Enceladus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enceladus_(moon) "Enceladus (moon)") (53), [Tethys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tethys_(moon) "Tethys (moon)") (50) and [Europa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa_(moon) "Europa (moon)") ([41](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Europa "List of craters on Europa")). For a full list, *see [List of craters in the Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_in_the_Solar_System "List of craters in the Solar System")*. The total number of craters on Mars greater than 1 kilometre in diameter is approximately 385,000, with 21% of those (~85,000) being over 3 kilometers in diameter.[[3]](#cite_note-3) The number of craters on Mars over 25 metres in diameter is suggested to be approximately 90 million.[[4]](#cite_note-4)

### Largest craters

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=List_of_craters_on_Mars&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Largest craters")]

Some of the largest craters on Mars remain unnamed. Diameters differ depending on source data. The largest confirmed impact basins on Mars are [Utopia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utopia_Planitia "Utopia Planitia") (buried, estimated diameter 3,300 km) [Hellas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hellas_Planitia "Hellas Planitia") (2,300 km), [Argyre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argyre_Planitia "Argyre Planitia") ( 1,800 km) and [Isidis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isidis_Planitia "Isidis Planitia") (1,500 km).

Appearance

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

* Lunar: 1,624 craters (31.2%)
* Martian: 1,092 craters (21.0%)

* Mercurian: 397 craters (7.6%)

Distribution of named [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") in the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") as of 2017.

This is a **list of craters on Mars**. [Impact craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars "Mars") larger than 1 km (0.62 mi) exist by the hundreds of thousands, but only about one thousand of them have names.[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-1) Names are assigned by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") after petitioning by relevant scientists, and in general, only craters that have a significant research interest are given names. Martian craters are named after famous scientists and [science fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_fiction "Science fiction") authors, or if less than 60 km (37 mi) in diameter, after towns on [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth"). Craters cannot be named for living people, and names for small craters are rarely intended to commemorate a specific town.[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Categories-2) Latitude and longitude are given as planetographic coordinates with west longitude.

## Statistics

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=List_of_craters_on_Mars&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Statistics")]

As of 2017, Martian craters account for 21% of all 5,211 named craters in the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System"). Apart from the [Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moon "Moon"), no other body has as many named craters as Mars. Other, non-planetary bodies with numerous named craters include [Callisto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Callisto_(moon) "Callisto (moon)") ([141](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Callisto "List of craters on Callisto")), [Ganymede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ganymede_(moon) "Ganymede (moon)") ([131](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Ganymede "List of craters on Ganymede")), [Rhea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhea_(moon) "Rhea (moon)") (128), [Vesta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4_Vesta "4 Vesta") (90), [Ceres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceres_(dwarf_planet) "Ceres (dwarf planet)") (90), [Dione](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dione_(moon) "Dione (moon)") (73), [Iapetus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iapetus_(moon) "Iapetus (moon)") (58), [Enceladus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enceladus_(moon) "Enceladus (moon)") (53), [Tethys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tethys_(moon) "Tethys (moon)") (50) and [Europa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa_(moon) "Europa (moon)") ([41](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Europa "List of craters on Europa")). For a full list, *see [List of craters in the Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_in_the_Solar_System "List of craters in the Solar System")*. The total number of craters on Mars greater than 1 kilometre in diameter is approximately 385,000, with 21% of those (~85,000) being over 3 kilometers in diameter.[[3]](#cite_note-3) The number of craters on Mars over 25 metres in diameter is suggested to be approximately 90 million.[[4]](#cite_note-4)

### Largest craters

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=List_of_craters_on_Mars&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Largest craters")]

Some of the largest craters on Mars remain unnamed. Diameters differ depending on source data. The largest confirmed impact basins on Mars are [Utopia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utopia_Planitia "Utopia Planitia") (buried, estimated diameter 3,300 km) [Hellas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hellas_Planitia "Hellas Planitia") (2,300 km), [Argyre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argyre_Planitia "Argyre Planitia") ( 1,800 km) and [Isidis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isidis_Planitia "Isidis Planitia") (1,500 km).

Appearance

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

* Lunar: 1,624 craters (31.2%)
* Martian: 1,092 craters (21.0%)
* Venusian: 900 craters (17.3%)
* Mercurian: 397 craters (7.6%)
* Others: 1,198 craters (23.0%)

Distribution of named [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") in the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") as of 2017.

This is a **list of craters on Mars**. [Impact craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars "Mars") larger than 1 km (0.62 mi) exist by the hundreds of thousands, but only about one thousand of them have names.[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-1) Names are assigned by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") after petitioning by relevant scientists, and in general, only craters that have a significant research interest are given names. Martian craters are named after famous scientists and [science fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_fiction "Science fiction") authors, or if less than 60 km (37 mi) in diameter, after towns on [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth"). Craters cannot be named for living people, and names for small craters are rarely intended to commemorate a specific town.[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Categories-2) Latitude and longitude are given as planetographic coordinates with west longitude.

## Statistics

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=List_of_craters_on_Mars&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Statistics")]

As of 2017, Martian craters account for 21% of all 5,211 named craters in the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System"). Apart from the [Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moon "Moon"), no other body has as many named craters as Mars. Other, non-planetary bodies with numerous named craters include [Callisto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Callisto_(moon) "Callisto (moon)") ([141](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Callisto "List of craters on Callisto")), [Ganymede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ganymede_(moon) "Ganymede (moon)") ([131](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Ganymede "List of craters on Ganymede")), [Rhea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhea_(moon) "Rhea (moon)") (128), [Vesta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4_Vesta "4 Vesta") (90), [Ceres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceres_(dwarf_planet) "Ceres (dwarf planet)") (90), [Dione](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dione_(moon) "Dione (moon)") (73), [Iapetus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iapetus_(moon) "Iapetus (moon)") (58), [Enceladus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enceladus_(moon) "Enceladus (moon)") (53), [Tethys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tethys_(moon) "Tethys (moon)") (50) and [Europa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa_(moon) "Europa (moon)") ([41](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Europa "List of craters on Europa")). For a full list, *see [List of craters in the Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_in_the_Solar_System "List of craters in the Solar System")*. The total number of craters on Mars greater than 1 kilometre in diameter is approximately 385,000, with 21% of those (~85,000) being over 3 kilometers in diameter.[[3]](#cite_note-3) The number of craters on Mars over 25 metres in diameter is suggested to be approximately 90 million.[[4]](#cite_note-4)

### Largest craters

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=List_of_craters_on_Mars&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Largest craters")]

Some of the largest craters on Mars remain unnamed. Diameters differ depending on source data. The largest confirmed impact basins on Mars are [Utopia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utopia_Planitia "Utopia Planitia") (buried, estimated diameter 3,300 km) [Hellas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hellas_Planitia "Hellas Planitia") (2,300 km), [Argyre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argyre_Planitia "Argyre Planitia") ( 1,800 km) and [Isidis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isidis_Planitia "Isidis Planitia") (1,500 km).

# A radiating beauty on Mars

![Becquerel Crater](https://media.esa.int/legacy/web/images/esa_multimedia/images/2013/09/becquerel_crater/13007492-1-eng-GB/154361/image-thumb__154361__fit_large/Becquerel_Crater.c8968fc4.webp)

ARCHIVE CONTENT   05 SEP. 2013 publication date   13875 Views

Exceptional structures deposited and shaped by water and winds adorn these interlocking craters and sculpt radiating patterns in the sands of Mars.

---

![]()

## Media modal

0 favorites   publication date   0 Views

![Becquerel Crater context](https://media.esa.int/legacy/web/images/esa_multimedia/images/2013/09/becquerel_crater_context/13007572-1-eng-GB/154390/image-thumb__154390__fit_medium/Becquerel_Crater_context.5c68f02f.webp)

Becquerel crater in context

This mosaic, which focuses on Becquerel crater in Arabia Terra, is composed of four images taken by the high-resolution stereo camera on ESA’s Mars Express. Arabia Terra is in the transition zone between the southern highlands and the northern lowlands of Mars.

Becquerel crater is named for the 19th-century French physicist Antoine Henri Becquerel (1852–1908), winner of the Nobel Prize in physics in 1903 along with Marie and Pierre Curie for the discovery of radioactivity.

It is the largest crater in this scene, with a diameter of 167 km, and drops to a depth of about 3.5 km below the surrounding terrain. A second large crater lies within Becquerel, punching even deeper into the surface, as seen in the Mars Express topography and 3D images.

---

![]()

## Media modal

0 favorites   publication date   0 Views

![Becquerel Crater topography](https://media.esa.int/legacy/web/images/esa_multimedia/images/2013/09/becquerel_crater_topography/13007683-1-eng-GB/153646/image-thumb__153646__fit_large/Becquerel_Crater_topography.b340f8bd.webp)

Becquerel crater topography

---

The perspective view below reveals an intriguing, large mound within Becquerel’s crater walls, reminiscent of Mount Sharp in Gale crater, currently being explored by NASA’s Curiosity rover.

The mound rises about 1 km above the crater floor and comprises hundreds of layers of light-toned sediments, each just a few metres thick, made of sulphate-bearing rocks. On Earth, sulphates are most often formed via the evaporation of water, so the presence of these minerals in Becquerel crater suggests that water may once have pooled here in a vast crater lake, before evaporating away.

---

![]()

## Media modal

0 favorites   publication date   0 Views

![Becquerel Crater sulphate mound](https://media.esa.int/legacy/web/images/esa_multimedia/images/2013/09/becquerel_crater_sulphate_mound/13007652-1-eng-GB/153623/image-thumb__153623__fit_large/Becquerel_Crater_sulphate_mound.be493ba5.webp)

Layered mound inside Becquerel crater

---

It is likely that the entire crater floor was once covered with such sediments, but over billions of years much of it has been eroded away by wind, leaving just a polished, rounded mound behind.

Similar light-toned sulphate-bearing deposits are seen all over Arabia Terra, including in the crater walls in this scene, pointing to a large-scale process that affected the entire region.

One popular theory is that large changes in the tilt of the rotational axis of Mars leads to significant changes in its climate, reflected in the thickness and repeating patterns found in the layers of sediment. A change in the environmental conditions would affect the way in which the sediments were initially deposited, as well as their subsequent resistance to erosion.

The deposits were laid down 3.8–3.5 billion years ago, at a time when Mars was evolving from a warm, wet world into the cold and dry planet we see today.

---

![]()

## Media modal

0 favorites   publication date   0 Views

![Becquerel Crater wind blown sediments](https://media.esa.int/legacy/web/images/esa_multimedia/images/2013/09/becquerel_crater_wind_blown_sediments/13007714-1-eng-GB/153660/image-thumb__153660__fit_large/Becquerel_Crater_wind_blown_sediments.09e0d9c3.webp)

Wind-blown sediments around Becquerel crater

---

Although water may no longer flow on the Red Planet, wind still plays a key role in shaping the environment. Dark dunes and wind-blown sediments streak through this scene, in vivid contrast to the bright mound.

Rather than having originated locally, the dark material inside Becquerel crater likely blew in from elsewhere – perhaps even from volcanic eruptions.

A dark streak seems to drag the material out from the craters in a wide swath towards the upper left of the main colour image (bottom right of the perspective view above). A number of tiny craters with tail-like structures lie along this track: their raised rims influence the flow of wind over them such that the material immediately downwind of the crater remains undisturbed in comparison to the surrounding, exposed plains.

Another streak of dust follows a radial path out of Becquerel crater; it likely traces out a gentle topographic depression, beyond the eroded rim of the neighbouring old crater.

Meanwhile, dark sediments inside the small crater towards the far left of the main image appear to have been blown out in a similar direction by the powerful prevailing wind.

---

![]()

## Media modal

0 favorites   publication date   0 Views

![Becquerel Crater 3D](https://media.esa.int/legacy/web/images/esa_multimedia/images/2013/09/becquerel_crater_3d/13007523-1-eng-GB/154381/image-thumb__154381__fit_large/Becquerel_Crater_3D.ef4ec181.webp)

Becquerel crater in 3D

---

These blowing sands continue to change the martian landscape even today, exposing ancient rock formations in some locations, while eradicating or covering younger features in others. Detailed studies of these wind-blown patterns can often yield interesting insights into the history of the Red Planet.

Although water may no longer flow on the Red Planet, wind still plays a key role in shaping the environment. Dark dunes and wind-blown sediments streak through this scene, in vivid contrast to the bright mound.

Rather than having originated locally, the dark material inside Becquerel crater likely blew in from elsewhere – perhaps even from volcanic eruptions.

A dark streak seems to drag the material out from the craters in a wide swath towards the upper left of the main colour image (bottom right of the perspective view above). A number of tiny craters with tail-like structures lie along this track: their raised rims influence the flow of wind over them such that the material immediately downwind of the crater remains undisturbed in comparison to the surrounding, exposed plains.

Another streak of dust follows a radial path out of Becquerel crater; it likely traces out a gentle topographic depression, beyond the eroded rim of the neighbouring old crater.

Meanwhile, dark sediments inside the small crater towards the far left of the main image appear to have been blown out in a similar direction by the powerful prevailing wind.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This article should list *only* official names approved by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") (IAU).[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-1)

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a4/Burns_cliff.jpg/250px-Burns_cliff.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Burns_cliff.jpg)

*[Opportunity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opportunity_(rover) "Opportunity (rover)")* rover images Burns Cliff inside [Endurance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endurance_(crater) "Endurance (crater)") [impact crater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") in 2004.

This is a partial [list of craters on Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars "List of craters on Mars"). There are hundreds of thousands of [impact craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars "Mars"), but only some of them have names. This list here only contains named Martian craters starting with the letter A – G *(see also lists for [H – N](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars:_H–N "List of craters on Mars: H–N") and [O – Z](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars:_O–Z "List of craters on Mars: O–Z"))*.

Large Martian craters (greater than 60 kilometers in diameter) are named after famous scientists and [science fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_fiction "Science fiction") authors; smaller ones (less than 60 km in diameter) get their names from towns on [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth"). Craters cannot be named for living people, and small crater names are not intended to be commemorative – that is, a small crater isn't actually named after a specific town on Earth, but rather its name comes at random from a pool of terrestrial place names, with some exceptions made for craters near landing sites.[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Categories-2) Latitude and longitude are given as planetographic coordinates with west longitude.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This article should list *only* official names approved by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") (IAU).[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-1)

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b4/Dinorwic_crater_area.png/250px-Dinorwic_crater_area.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dinorwic_crater_area.png)

The crater [Nhill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nhill_(crater) "Nhill (crater)") and its surroundings, in a screenshot in [NASA World Wind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA_World_Wind "NASA World Wind")

This is a partial [list of craters on Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars "List of craters on Mars"). There are hundreds of thousands of [impact craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars "Mars"), but only some of them have names. This list here only contains named Martian craters starting with the letter H – N *(see also lists for [A – G](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars:_A–G "List of craters on Mars: A–G") and [O – Z](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars:_O–Z "List of craters on Mars: O–Z"))*.

Large Martian craters (greater than 60 kilometers in diameter) are named after famous scientists and [science fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_fiction "Science fiction") authors; smaller ones (less than 60 km in diameter) get their names from towns on [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth"). Craters cannot be named for living people, and small crater names are not intended to be commemorative – that is, a small crater isn't named after a specific town on Earth, but rather its name comes at random from a pool of terrestrial place names, with some exceptions made for craters near landing sites.[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Categories-2) Latitude and longitude are given as planetographic coordinates with west longitude.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This article should list *only* official names approved by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") (IAU).[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-1)

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a4/Burns_cliff.jpg/250px-Burns_cliff.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Burns_cliff.jpg)

*[Opportunity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opportunity_(rover) "Opportunity (rover)")* rover images Burns Cliff inside [Endurance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endurance_(crater) "Endurance (crater)") [impact crater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") in 2004.

This is a partial [list of craters on Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars "List of craters on Mars"). There are hundreds of thousands of [impact craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars "Mars"), but only some of them have names. This list here only contains named Martian craters starting with the letter A – G *(see also lists for [H – N](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars:_H–N "List of craters on Mars: H–N") and [O – Z](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars:_O–Z "List of craters on Mars: O–Z"))*.

Large Martian craters (greater than 60 kilometers in diameter) are named after famous scientists and [science fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_fiction "Science fiction") authors; smaller ones (less than 60 km in diameter) get their names from towns on [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth"). Craters cannot be named for living people, and small crater names are not intended to be commemorative – that is, a small crater isn't actually named after a specific town on Earth, but rather its name comes at random from a pool of terrestrial place names, with some exceptions made for craters near landing sites.[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Categories-2) Latitude and longitude are given as planetographic coordinates with west longitude.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This article should list *only* official names approved by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") (IAU).[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-1)

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b4/Dinorwic_crater_area.png/250px-Dinorwic_crater_area.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dinorwic_crater_area.png)

The crater [Nhill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nhill_(crater) "Nhill (crater)") and its surroundings, in a screenshot in [NASA World Wind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA_World_Wind "NASA World Wind")

This is a partial [list of craters on Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars "List of craters on Mars"). There are hundreds of thousands of [impact craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars "Mars"), but only some of them have names. This list here only contains named Martian craters starting with the letter H – N *(see also lists for [A – G](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars:_A–G "List of craters on Mars: A–G") and [O – Z](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars:_O–Z "List of craters on Mars: O–Z"))*.

Large Martian craters (greater than 60 kilometers in diameter) are named after famous scientists and [science fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_fiction "Science fiction") authors; smaller ones (less than 60 km in diameter) get their names from towns on [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth"). Craters cannot be named for living people, and small crater names are not intended to be commemorative – that is, a small crater isn't named after a specific town on Earth, but rather its name comes at random from a pool of terrestrial place names, with some exceptions made for craters near landing sites.[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Categories-2) Latitude and longitude are given as planetographic coordinates with west longitude.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This article should list *only* official names approved by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") (IAU).[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-1)

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a4/Burns_cliff.jpg/250px-Burns_cliff.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Burns_cliff.jpg)

*[Opportunity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opportunity_(rover) "Opportunity (rover)")* rover images Burns Cliff inside [Endurance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endurance_(crater) "Endurance (crater)") [impact crater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") in 2004.

This is a partial [list of craters on Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars "List of craters on Mars"). There are hundreds of thousands of [impact craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars "Mars"), but only some of them have names. This list here only contains named Martian craters starting with the letter A – G *(see also lists for [H – N](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars:_H–N "List of craters on Mars: H–N") and [O – Z](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars:_O–Z "List of craters on Mars: O–Z"))*.

Large Martian craters (greater than 60 kilometers in diameter) are named after famous scientists and [science fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_fiction "Science fiction") authors; smaller ones (less than 60 km in diameter) get their names from towns on [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth"). Craters cannot be named for living people, and small crater names are not intended to be commemorative – that is, a small crater isn't actually named after a specific town on Earth, but rather its name comes at random from a pool of terrestrial place names, with some exceptions made for craters near landing sites.[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Categories-2) Latitude and longitude are given as planetographic coordinates with west longitude.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This article should list *only* official names approved by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") (IAU).[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-1)

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b4/Dinorwic_crater_area.png/250px-Dinorwic_crater_area.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dinorwic_crater_area.png)

The crater [Nhill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nhill_(crater) "Nhill (crater)") and its surroundings, in a screenshot in [NASA World Wind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA_World_Wind "NASA World Wind")

This is a partial [list of craters on Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars "List of craters on Mars"). There are hundreds of thousands of [impact craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars "Mars"), but only some of them have names. This list here only contains named Martian craters starting with the letter H – N *(see also lists for [A – G](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars:_A–G "List of craters on Mars: A–G") and [O – Z](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars:_O–Z "List of craters on Mars: O–Z"))*.

Large Martian craters (greater than 60 kilometers in diameter) are named after famous scientists and [science fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_fiction "Science fiction") authors; smaller ones (less than 60 km in diameter) get their names from towns on [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth"). Craters cannot be named for living people, and small crater names are not intended to be commemorative – that is, a small crater isn't named after a specific town on Earth, but rather its name comes at random from a pool of terrestrial place names, with some exceptions made for craters near landing sites.[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Categories-2) Latitude and longitude are given as planetographic coordinates with west longitude.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This article should list *only* official names approved by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") (IAU).[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-1)

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a4/Burns_cliff.jpg/250px-Burns_cliff.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Burns_cliff.jpg)

*[Opportunity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opportunity_(rover) "Opportunity (rover)")* rover images Burns Cliff inside [Endurance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endurance_(crater) "Endurance (crater)") [impact crater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") in 2004.

This is a partial [list of craters on Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars "List of craters on Mars"). There are hundreds of thousands of [impact craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars "Mars"), but only some of them have names. This list here only contains named Martian craters starting with the letter A – G *(see also lists for [H – N](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars:_H–N "List of craters on Mars: H–N") and [O – Z](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars:_O–Z "List of craters on Mars: O–Z"))*.

Large Martian craters (greater than 60 kilometers in diameter) are named after famous scientists and [science fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_fiction "Science fiction") authors; smaller ones (less than 60 km in diameter) get their names from towns on [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth"). Craters cannot be named for living people, and small crater names are not intended to be commemorative – that is, a small crater isn't actually named after a specific town on Earth, but rather its name comes at random from a pool of terrestrial place names, with some exceptions made for craters near landing sites.[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Categories-2) Latitude and longitude are given as planetographic coordinates with west longitude.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This article should list *only* official names approved by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") (IAU).[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-1)

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b4/Dinorwic_crater_area.png/250px-Dinorwic_crater_area.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dinorwic_crater_area.png)

The crater [Nhill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nhill_(crater) "Nhill (crater)") and its surroundings, in a screenshot in [NASA World Wind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA_World_Wind "NASA World Wind")

This is a partial [list of craters on Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars "List of craters on Mars"). There are hundreds of thousands of [impact craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars "Mars"), but only some of them have names. This list here only contains named Martian craters starting with the letter H – N *(see also lists for [A – G](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars:_A–G "List of craters on Mars: A–G") and [O – Z](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars:_O–Z "List of craters on Mars: O–Z"))*.

Large Martian craters (greater than 60 kilometers in diameter) are named after famous scientists and [science fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_fiction "Science fiction") authors; smaller ones (less than 60 km in diameter) get their names from towns on [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth"). Craters cannot be named for living people, and small crater names are not intended to be commemorative – that is, a small crater isn't named after a specific town on Earth, but rather its name comes at random from a pool of terrestrial place names, with some exceptions made for craters near landing sites.[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Categories-2) Latitude and longitude are given as planetographic coordinates with west longitude.

You are a web search agent. Follow your search method.

## Search method v007

Define X and Y exactly, including entity unit, exclusions, effective dates, eligible subtypes and group-membership rules. Start sequentially with one X-only search, one Y-only search and one conjunction search, using the user's broad predicate wording rather than a familiar subtype. Maintain deduplicated X/Y frontiers and an identity/evidence ledger. Also maintain a compact scope ledger: for each discovery query record added restrictions not required by the hunt (subtype, occupation, geography, era, source or familiar-name terms). A successful restricted query does not establish coverage of its parent category. Derive a few meaningful sibling partitions from source taxonomies or the eligibility definition; do not invent an exhaustive cross-product or enumerate a whole census by default. Run short discovery/check rounds, prioritizing expected verified additions per total resolution cost. Each round's neglected-subtype or reverse-frontier probe must address a specific untested scope-ledger cell or remove a recorded accidental restriction; merely paraphrasing a prior conjunction does not qualify. Check source-backed candidates on Parallel for only unresolved predicates, supplying identity and existing evidence. Use small affordable batches, price every candidate, and do not recheck established facts. No result means unresolved, not false; reject only on contradiction or an exhaustive applicable source. Escalate promising ambiguous or conflicting cases individually to Exa. After two discovery searches add no plausible identities, prohibit synonymous conjunction searches and perform a residual-scope pass: identify the most consequential restriction accumulated so far, try a sibling subtype or unrestricted parent on the opposite frontier, then resolve resulting candidates before further discovery. Reserve at least 35% of initial funds for evidence and stop discovery whenever pending checks require the remaining funds. Before submitting with spare funds, perform up to three affordable residual probes covering distinct untested restrictions or source partitions, retaining enough funds to verify their likely candidates. Stop this pass after two probes add neither candidates nor useful evidence; do not spend merely to exhaust the budget. Finish with identity, predicate, subtype and effective-date audits; submit supported intersections only and never infer completeness from saturation.

### Routing policy
Default route: providers ['parallel'], tier default, 8 results per provider.
check_candidates route: ['parallel'].
Parallel alone, default tier, 8 results for baseline and residual discovery, 4 for exact missing-fact checks. No routine also variants or broad auto-routing. Price candidate batches as the sum of queries and provider charges; fewer results are not presumed cheaper. Exa alone with 4 results for selected unresolved identities where ambiguity, conflicting evidence or inaccessibility warrants the higher cost. At most one initial Exa discovery probe after Parallel stagnation, continued only if it contributes useful new identities or evidence. Try a genuinely different scope partition on Parallel before buying provider diversity for a repetitive query. Authoritative-domain filters are for targeted evidence, not general frontier coverage; relax failed filters. Use publication-date filters only when publication date itself determines eligibility, and verify effective dates in content.

### Fetch policy
Reuse cached source facts. Fetch authoritative pages that can settle missing identity or predicates, and useful multi-candidate lists, rather than every result. When a list is used for scope coverage, inspect its stated subtype, date range and pagination/section links; an excerpt or one section is not an exhausted category. Follow only sections tied to a promising uncovered partition, without committing to bulk census extraction. After a blocked or uninformative page, make one targeted alternate-source attempt rather than a fetch chain.

You have $0.08 of Telem search budget. Every tool result reports what is left. When the budget runs out or you are done, call submit. Only submit items you have evidence for. Each find must cite a URL retrieved during this search whose text names the item; otherwise it scores as wrong.

- If a Nix dependency becomes useful for recurring or future work, tell the human and suggest adding it to the appropriate durable Nix configuration (such as a project flake/dev shell, Home Manager, or nix-darwin configuration). Do not make that durable change unless asked.

Distribution of named [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") in the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") as of 2017.

This is a **list of craters on Mars**. [Impact craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars "Mars") larger than 1 km (0.62 mi) exist by the hundreds of thousands, but only about one thousand of them have names.[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-1) Names are assigned by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") after petitioning by relevant scientists, and in general, only craters that have a significant research interest are given names. Martian craters are named after famous scientists and [science fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_fiction "Science fiction") authors, or if less than 60 km (37 mi) in diameter, after towns on [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth"). Craters cannot be named for living people, and names for small craters are rarely intended to commemorate a specific town.[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Categories-2) Latitude and longitude are given as planetographic coordinates with west longitude.

## Statistics

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=List_of_craters_on_Mars&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Statistics")]

As of 2017, Martian craters account for 21% of all 5,211 named craters in the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System"). Apart from the [Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moon "Moon"), no other body has as many named craters as Mars. Other, non-planetary bodies with numerous named craters include [Callisto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Callisto_(moon) "Callisto (moon)") ([141](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Callisto "List of craters on Callisto")), [Ganymede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ganymede_(moon) "Ganymede (moon)") ([131](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Ganymede "List of craters on Ganymede")), [Rhea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhea_(moon) "Rhea (moon)") (128), [Vesta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4_Vesta "4 Vesta") (90), [Ceres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceres_(dwarf_planet) "Ceres (dwarf planet)") (90), [Dione](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dione_(moon) "Dione (moon)") (73), [Iapetus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iapetus_(moon) "Iapetus (moon)") (58), [Enceladus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enceladus_(moon) "Enceladus (moon)") (53), [Tethys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tethys_(moon) "Tethys (moon)") (50) and [Europa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa_(moon) "Europa (moon)") ([41](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Europa "List of craters on Europa")). For a full list, *see [List of craters in the Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_in_the_Solar_System "List of craters in the Solar System")*. The total number of craters on Mars greater than 1 kilometre in diameter is approximately 385,000, with 21% of those (~85,000) being over 3 kilometers in diameter.[[3]](#cite_note-3) The number of craters on Mars over 25 metres in diameter is suggested to be approximately 90 million.[[4]](#cite_note-4)

### Largest craters

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=List_of_craters_on_Mars&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Largest craters")]

Some of the largest craters on Mars remain unnamed. Diameters differ depending on source data. The largest confirmed impact basins on Mars are [Utopia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utopia_Planitia "Utopia Planitia") (buried, estimated diameter 3,300 km) [Hellas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hellas_Planitia "Hellas Planitia") (2,300 km), [Argyre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argyre_Planitia "Argyre Planitia") ( 1,800 km) and [Isidis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isidis_Planitia "Isidis Planitia") (1,500 km).

# A radiating beauty on Mars

![Becquerel Crater](https://media.esa.int/legacy/web/images/esa_multimedia/images/2013/09/becquerel_crater/13007492-1-eng-GB/154361/image-thumb__154361__fit_large/Becquerel_Crater.c8968fc4.webp)

ARCHIVE CONTENT   05 SEP. 2013 publication date   13875 Views

Exceptional structures deposited and shaped by water and winds adorn these interlocking craters and sculpt radiating patterns in the sands of Mars.

---

![]()

## Media modal

0 favorites   publication date   0 Views

![Becquerel Crater context](https://media.esa.int/legacy/web/images/esa_multimedia/images/2013/09/becquerel_crater_context/13007572-1-eng-GB/154390/image-thumb__154390__fit_medium/Becquerel_Crater_context.5c68f02f.webp)

Becquerel crater in context

This mosaic, which focuses on Becquerel crater in Arabia Terra, is composed of four images taken by the high-resolution stereo camera on ESA’s Mars Express. Arabia Terra is in the transition zone between the southern highlands and the northern lowlands of Mars.

Becquerel crater is named for the 19th-century French physicist Antoine Henri Becquerel (1852–1908), winner of the Nobel Prize in physics in 1903 along with Marie and Pierre Curie for the discovery of radioactivity.

It is the largest crater in this scene, with a diameter of 167 km, and drops to a depth of about 3.5 km below the surrounding terrain. A second large crater lies within Becquerel, punching even deeper into the surface, as seen in the Mars Express topography and 3D images.

---

![]()

## Media modal

0 favorites   publication date   0 Views

![Becquerel Crater topography](https://media.esa.int/legacy/web/images/esa_multimedia/images/2013/09/becquerel_crater_topography/13007683-1-eng-GB/153646/image-thumb__153646__fit_large/Becquerel_Crater_topography.b340f8bd.webp)

Becquerel crater topography

---

The perspective view below reveals an intriguing, large mound within Becquerel’s crater walls, reminiscent of Mount Sharp in Gale crater, currently being explored by NASA’s Curiosity rover.

The mound rises about 1 km above the crater floor and comprises hundreds of layers of light-toned sediments, each just a few metres thick, made of sulphate-bearing rocks. On Earth, sulphates are most often formed via the evaporation of water, so the presence of these minerals in Becquerel crater suggests that water may once have pooled here in a vast crater lake, before evaporating away.

---

![]()

## Media modal

0 favorites   publication date   0 Views

![Becquerel Crater sulphate mound](https://media.esa.int/legacy/web/images/esa_multimedia/images/2013/09/becquerel_crater_sulphate_mound/13007652-1-eng-GB/153623/image-thumb__153623__fit_large/Becquerel_Crater_sulphate_mound.be493ba5.webp)

Layered mound inside Becquerel crater

---

It is likely that the entire crater floor was once covered with such sediments, but over billions of years much of it has been eroded away by wind, leaving just a polished, rounded mound behind.

Similar light-toned sulphate-bearing deposits are seen all over Arabia Terra, including in the crater walls in this scene, pointing to a large-scale process that affected the entire region.

One popular theory is that large changes in the tilt of the rotational axis of Mars leads to significant changes in its climate, reflected in the thickness and repeating patterns found in the layers of sediment. A change in the environmental conditions would affect the way in which the sediments were initially deposited, as well as their subsequent resistance to erosion.

The deposits were laid down 3.8–3.5 billion years ago, at a time when Mars was evolving from a warm, wet world into the cold and dry planet we see today.

---

## Media modal

0 favorites   publication date   0 Views

![Becquerel Crater wind blown sediments](https://media.esa.int/legacy/web/images/esa_multimedia/images/2013/09/becquerel_crater_wind_blown_sediments/13007714-1-eng-GB/153660/image-thumb__153660__fit_large/Becquerel_Crater_wind_blown_sediments.09e0d9c3.webp)

Wind-blown sediments around Becquerel crater

---

Although water may no longer flow on the Red Planet, wind still plays a key role in shaping the environment. Dark dunes and wind-blown sediments streak through this scene, in vivid contrast to the bright mound.

Rather than having originated locally, the dark material inside Becquerel crater likely blew in from elsewhere – perhaps even from volcanic eruptions.

A dark streak seems to drag the material out from the craters in a wide swath towards the upper left of the main colour image (bottom right of the perspective view above). A number of tiny craters with tail-like structures lie along this track: their raised rims influence the flow of wind over them such that the material immediately downwind of the crater remains undisturbed in comparison to the surrounding, exposed plains.

Another streak of dust follows a radial path out of Becquerel crater; it likely traces out a gentle topographic depression, beyond the eroded rim of the neighbouring old crater.

Meanwhile, dark sediments inside the small crater towards the far left of the main image appear to have been blown out in a similar direction by the powerful prevailing wind.

---

These blowing sands continue to change the martian landscape even today, exposing ancient rock formations in some locations, while eradicating or covering younger features in others. Detailed studies of these wind-blown patterns can often yield interesting insights into the history of the Red Planet.

Appearance

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This article should list *only* official names approved by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") (IAU).[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-1)

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a4/Burns_cliff.jpg/250px-Burns_cliff.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Burns_cliff.jpg)

*[Opportunity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opportunity_(rover) "Opportunity (rover)")* rover images Burns Cliff inside [Endurance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endurance_(crater) "Endurance (crater)") [impact crater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") in 2004.

This is a partial [list of craters on Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars "List of craters on Mars"). There are hundreds of thousands of [impact craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars "Mars"), but only some of them have names. This list here only contains named Martian craters starting with the letter A – G *(see also lists for [H – N](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars:_H–N "List of craters on Mars: H–N") and [O – Z](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars:_O–Z "List of craters on Mars: O–Z"))*.

Large Martian craters (greater than 60 kilometers in diameter) are named after famous scientists and [science fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_fiction "Science fiction") authors; smaller ones (less than 60 km in diameter) get their names from towns on [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth"). Craters cannot be named for living people, and small crater names are not intended to be commemorative – that is, a small crater isn't actually named after a specific town on Earth, but rather its name comes at random from a pool of terrestrial place names, with some exceptions made for craters near landing sites.[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Categories-2) Latitude and longitude are given as planetographic coordinates with west longitude.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This article should list *only* official names approved by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") (IAU).[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-1)

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b4/Dinorwic_crater_area.png/250px-Dinorwic_crater_area.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dinorwic_crater_area.png)

The crater [Nhill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nhill_(crater) "Nhill (crater)") and its surroundings, in a screenshot in [NASA World Wind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA_World_Wind "NASA World Wind")

This is a partial [list of craters on Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars "List of craters on Mars"). There are hundreds of thousands of [impact craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars "Mars"), but only some of them have names. This list here only contains named Martian craters starting with the letter H – N *(see also lists for [A – G](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars:_A–G "List of craters on Mars: A–G") and [O – Z](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars:_O–Z "List of craters on Mars: O–Z"))*.

Large Martian craters (greater than 60 kilometers in diameter) are named after famous scientists and [science fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_fiction "Science fiction") authors; smaller ones (less than 60 km in diameter) get their names from towns on [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth"). Craters cannot be named for living people, and small crater names are not intended to be commemorative – that is, a small crater isn't named after a specific town on Earth, but rather its name comes at random from a pool of terrestrial place names, with some exceptions made for craters near landing sites.[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Categories-2) Latitude and longitude are given as planetographic coordinates with west longitude.
